abstract: People in developed countries spend over 90% of their time in built environments. Yet, we know little about its pervasive and often hidden effects on our mental state and our brain. Despite growing interest in the neuroscience of architecture, much of this scholarship has been descriptive. The typical approach is to map knowledge of the brain onto constructs important to architecture. For a programmatic line of research, how might descriptive neuroarchitecture be transformed into an experimen- tal science? We review the literature outlining how one might consider experimental architecture first by examining the role of natural features in architectural settings. We then turn to the human experience of occupants, and hypothesized that aesthetic responses to architectural interiors reduce to key psychological dimensions. Conducting Psychometric Network Analysis (PNA) and Principal Components Analysis (PCA) on responses to curated images, we identified three components: coherence (ease of organizing and comprehending a scene), fascination (informational richness and generated interest), and hominess (personal ease and comfort). Coherence and fascination are well-established dimensions for natural scenes. Hominess was a new dimension related to architectural interiors. Central to all three communities in the PNA was emotional valence. We also reanalyzed data from an earlier fMRI study in which participants made beauty and approach-avoidance decisions while viewing the same images. Regardless of task, the degree of fascination covaried with neural activity in the right lingual gyrus. In contrast, coherence covaried with neural activity in the left inferior occipital gyrus only when participants judged beauty, and hominess covaried with neural activity in the left cuneus only when they made approach-avoidance decisions. The visual brain harbours hidden sensitivities to architectural interiors that are captured by the dimensions of coherence, fascination, and hominess. These findings represent first steps towards an experimental neuroarchitecture.

methodology.design: Psychometric Network Analysis (PNA) and Principal Components Analysis (PCA)

methodology.study_name: Reanalysis of Vartanian et al. (2013) fMRI study
methodology.design: Integration of PCA scores (from Coburn et al., 2020) with fMRI data

sample.sample_size: Participants (number not specified) evaluated 200 interior architectural scenes, yielding thousands of ratings across 16 psychological responses.
A different group of participants (number not specified in this paper) from the Coburn et al. (2020) study.

manipulated_features: Natural features in architectural settings (plants, water features, small fires, large windows, balconies, pictures/photographs of outdoors)
Implicit naturalness (high densities of natural visual patterns, edge density, contrast)
Shape and undulation of the skyline
Presence of water in the scene
outcomes: Emotional valence (basic assessment of how the space makes viewers feel)

Neural activity (anterior cingulate activation, right lingual gyrus, left inferior occipital gyrus, left cuneus, parahippocampus place area (PPA) activation, temporal lobe structures, primary visual cortex, anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC))
key_findings: People in developed countries spend over 90% of their time in built environments, and aesthetic qualities of the built environment deeply influence psychological states.

**From Coburn et al. (2020) study**: Nearly 90% of the variance in responses to architectural interiors was explained by three underlying psychological dimensions: coherence, fascination, and hominess.
Coherence was defined as the ease of organizing and comprehending a scene.
Fascination was defined as informational richness and generated interest.
Hominess was defined as personal ease and comfort, identified as a new dimension related to architectural interiors.
Emotional valence was central to all three psychological dimensions (coherence, fascination, hominess) in the Psychometric Network Analysis.
**From reanalysis of Vartanian et al. (2013) fMRI data**: The degree of fascination covaried with neural activity in the right lingual gyrus for both beauty judgment and approach-avoidance tasks.
Coherence covaried with neural activity in the left inferior occipital gyrus only when participants judged beauty.
Hominess covaried with neural activity in the left cuneus only when participants made approach-avoidance decisions.
The visual brain harbours hidden sensitivities to architectural interiors that are captured by the dimensions of coherence, fascination, and hominess.
Increased anterior cingulate activation was observed when participants made judgments of interior spaces during fMRI (Vartanian et al., 2013).
High densities of natural visual patterns (edge density, contrast) explained most of the variance in preference ratings for both architectural facades and interior scenes (Coburn et al., 2019).
Curvilinear spaces were preferred over straight edges (Vartanian et al., 2013).
Parahippocampus place area (PPA) activation was influenced by the openness of a space, regardless of whether the space was natural or human-made (Kravitz et al., 2011).
Open interior spaces were rated as more natural (Coburn et al., 2019) and beautiful (Vartanian et al., 2015), and were preferred over closed ones (Dosen and Ostwald, 2016).
Fractals evoke feelings of naturalness and are preferred over non-fractal design (Joye, 2007; Lavdas and Schirpke, 2020; Taylor, 2021).
Neurons in primary visual cortex show preferential responses to fractals (Yu et al., 2005).
Decodable neural representations of architectural styles and buildings were found in high-level visual regions, but not in primary visual cortex (Choo et al., 2017).

High-level scene features (shape/undulation of skyline, water presence, building distribution) mediated the relationship between low-level scene features and aesthetic preference ratings, explaining over half of their shared statistical variance (Ibarra et al., 2017).
The anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) was engaged when people viewed enclosed interior spaces that elicited exit decisions (Vartanian et al., 2015).
Heightened fear, stress, and cortisol levels were observed when people were immersed in a virtual simulation of an enclosed room (Fich et al., 2014).

Prefrontal and hippocampal brain regions are involved in beauty judgments of architecture, suggesting conscious reasoning and memory retrieval influence emotional reactions (Coburn et al., 2017; Vartanian et al., 2013; Kirk et al., 2009).
mechanisms: **Attention Restoration Theory (ART)**: Nature offloads effortful cognitive processing, leading to improved ability to focus by reducing the burden on directed attention.
**Stress-Reduction Framework**: Unthreatening settings (open, calm, warm) reduce stress by influencing cortisol response and the baseline tone of the parasympathetic autonomic nervous system.
**Prospect-Refuge theory**: Environments that offer both openness (prospect) and feelings of safety (refuge) were evolutionarily beneficial, leading to aesthetic preference.

**Fractals**: The visual system is proficient at grouping repeating elements and processes fractals automatically and fluently; neurons in primary visual cortex show preferential responses to fractals, adapting the visual system to the natural environment.

**Aesthetic Triad (Neuroarchitecture model)**: Human-building interactions are mediated by three large-scale neural networks: sensory-motor (bottom-up processing of features), knowledge-meaning (top-down processing, influenced by cultural background, identity, education), and emotion-valuation (integrates information from the other two systems, leading to aesthetic experiences).

**aMCC activation**: The anterior midcingulate cortex receives projections from the amygdala, indicating a potential role in fear-processing for negative emotions related to architectural spaces, particularly those from which people wish to depart.
limitations: Architectural spaces encompass a wide range of functions and settings, so features related to aesthetic experience may not be universally shared.
Practical limitations (physical and financial constraints) limit potential design choices.
The function of a space (e.g., hospital, school, home) cannot be overlooked, complicating generalization of findings.
Design elements that foster wellness are unlikely to be consistent across different settings, making broad generalizations difficult.
Most neuroarchitecture studies use 2-D images, which overlooks features like scale and texture, denies movement, and introduces confounds, limiting generalizability.
Buildings are three-dimensional, immersive, interactive, and multisensory; images cannot adequately convey contextual (e.g., outside noise, surrounding environment) and functional factors.
Virtual reality can mitigate some problems but may not fully capture the multidimensional and multimodal experience of architecture.

Temporal dynamics of aesthetic experiences are often overlooked; most studies present images for only a few seconds, but aesthetic experiences vary over longer durations (e.g., repeated viewings can lead to more positive appraisals), raising methodological and theoretical issues.
design_implications: Incorporate natural features directly into built environments (plants, water features, small fires).
Incorporate large windows or balconies that provide extensive vistas of the outdoors.
Arrange pictures or photographs of the outdoors around an interior.
Incorporate patterns that occur frequently in nature into design (e.g., high densities of natural visual patterns, curvilinear spaces, fractals).
Design buildings to increase the baseline tone of the parasympathetic autonomic nervous system to reduce stress.
Design buildings and urban environments informed by the three psychological dimensions of coherence, fascination, and hominess.
